audit.reasoning: The classification (tonal; six lexical tones; no word-stress rule, 'unstressed' used only for function words in connected speech and medial syllables of Pali loans) rests on Morey 2005 PL-565, the standard reference grammar by the primary fieldworker, held as the publisher's open text layer; I re-opened it and every quoted fragment is verbatim at the stated sections/pages (pp.122, 127, 134). Glottolog's per-language list offers only Thai-university theses and a 9-pp conference phonology paper, none superior. Open instrumental/tonal literature fetched sources now (Rose 1990 SST; Morey 2005 LTBA, scanned; Morey 2020 Himalayan Linguistics) uniformly describes a six-tone system with contrastive creak and says nothing about word stress, confirming the coding. No StressTyp2/WALS conflict exists. Nothing found suggests a recode; wishlist items are low-priority confirmations only.

sources.citation: Morey, Stephen. 2020. Syllable duration in Tai Phake: The interaction between vowel length and tone length. Himalayan Linguistics 19(2): 69-79. DOI 10.5070/H91150963.
sources.quote: 'Tai Phake (Tai Kadai/Southwestern Tai) has six lexical tones, and nine phonemic vowels plus a length distinction between /a/ and /aː/ ... Tone 3 is creaky and is primarily distinguished from the others by phonation. Tone 4 is mid falling and short, whereas Tone 5 is mid falling and longer.' No occurrence of stress/accent/prominence anywhere in the paper (grep).

sources.citation: Morey, Stephen. 2005. Tonal change in the Tai languages of Northeast India. Linguistics of the Tibeto-Burman Area 28(2): 139-202. (SEAlang SALA archive scan; image-only, scanned at 200 dpi, one tesseract).
sources.quote: 'After working in Namphakey and in several other Phake villages, I found that the distribution of the tones was exactly as Banchob had described (Morey 2005).' Phake treated purely as a six-tone system; the only 'stress' mentions concern Aiton and the Khamti script, not Phake.
sources.locator: sec. 3.1 Phake, pp.158-161 (Tables 7-9 Phake tone box); stress hits only p.164 (Aiton rising allotone 'in stressed positions') and p.166 (Khamti revised script 'Tone marks 1 & 2 are reserved for unstressed tones')

sources.citation: Rose, Phil. 1990. Thai-Phake tones: acoustic, aerodynamic and perceptual data on a Tai dialect with contrastive creak. In R. Seidl (ed.), Proc. 3rd Australian International Conference on Speech Science and Technology (SST-90), 388-393 (author's site lists 394-399). ASSTA.
sources.quote: 'In unstopped syllables, TP contrasts 6 tones, while in stopped syllables only a two-way contrast obtains ... perhaps the most interesting way in which TP differs phonologically from other Tai varieties is in the contrastive use of a creaky phonation type to distinguish the sixth tone.' Instrumental (F0, amplitude, duration, airflow) study of citation monosyllables, one speaker; no mention of stress/accent (grep).
